entries.short_definition: An emotion often associated with loss, separation, disappointment, or unmet hopes.

entries.definition: For example, someone may feel shame about feeling afraid. Distinguishing the initial feeling from reactions to it can clarify what needs validation, a different interpretation, or another skill.

references.author: Marsha M. Linehan
references.title: DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015)

entries.short_definition: An emotional response that develops in reaction to another emotional experience.

entries.definition: In ACT, self-as-context involves noticing experience without reducing your identity to one thought, feeling, role, or story. It does not require becoming detached or losing contact with the present situation.

entries.short_definition: The perspective from which you notice changing thoughts, feelings, and experiences.

entries.definition: Consider how to be fair to yourself and others, truthful, and consistent with your values. Keeping self-respect can matter even when you do not obtain the response you hoped for.

entries.definition: Choose sights, sounds, textures, tastes, or scents that are safe and personally soothing. Different people find different sensations helpful; comfort is not something you have to earn.

entries.short_definition: Using comforting sensory experiences to support yourself through distress.

entries.definition: Self-validation acknowledges feelings, needs, and relevant circumstances while leaving room to correct mistakes. It supports self-respect without requiring the conclusion that every interpretation or action was justified.

entries.definition: Shame often brings an urge to hide or withdraw. It can be shaped by invalidation or harsh standards and does not establish that you are defective. Examine the facts and seek a response that protects dignity.

entries.definition: Regular routines and a suitable sleep environment are parts of this DBT skill area. Sleep difficulties have many possible causes; habits can support care without guaranteeing sleep or replacing assessment when problems persist.

entries.definition: STOP prompts you to pause, gain some distance, notice what is happening, and choose your next action deliberately. It helps create space between an urge and a response.

entries.short_definition: A DBT pause skill for interrupting an impulsive response.

entries.definition: DBT describes facial cooling as a way to engage a physiological settling response. Cold exposure can affect heart rate and has medical precautions; consult the full guidance before trying it rather than using a glossary definition as instructions.

entries.short_definition: The temperature component of TIPP, using facial cooling to influence arousal.

entries.definition: TIPP groups temperature, intense exercise, paced breathing, and muscle relaxation. Linehan calls the group TIP. Choose a method suited to your health and circumstances; these skills have physical precautions and are not all suitable for everyone.

entries.short_definition: Body-focused DBT skills that can help reduce intense emotional arousal.

entries.definition: Choosing acceptance is not the same as already feeling accepting. Turning the mind is a repeated orientation toward reality that may be needed many times in the same difficult situation.

references.title: DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015)

entries.short_definition: Renewing the choice to move toward acceptance when you notice resistance.

entries.definition: An underlying assumption connects a condition with an expected result, such as expecting rejection whenever you disagree. Treating the rule as a testable prediction can reveal where it fits and where it is too rigid.

references.title: Mind Over Mood, Second Edition

entries.short_definition: A personal rule or prediction that guides how you respond.

entries.definition: Attend to an urge as an experience that can change over time. The aim is to allow room for choice, not to guarantee that the urge disappears quickly. Additional support may still be needed.

entries.short_definition: Noticing the rise and fall of an urge without automatically acting on it.

entries.definition: Validation can recognise a feeling in light of a person's circumstances without endorsing an inaccurate belief or harmful action. Careful listening and checking your understanding matter more than assuming you already know.

references.title: DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015)

entries.short_definition: Acknowledging what is understandable or accurate in someone's experience.

entries.definition: Values describe how you want to act, such as with care or curiosity. A goal can be completed; a value can guide many different actions over time. DBT also uses values to guide longer-term goals and the actions that build a meaningful life.

entries.definition: Illness, exhaustion, accumulated stress, and other circumstances may lower available coping capacity. Identifying these factors suggests places to add care or support; it does not make a harmful response inevitable.

entries.definition: The middle path brings acceptance and change into the same response. It is not automatically a halfway compromise: the aim is a fuller understanding that leads to effective action.

entries.definition: Willfulness can appear as refusing to act, giving up, or trying to force everything to go your way. In DBT it names a changeable response, not a bad identity. Notice it without adding shame.

entries.definition: The practice explores how body posture and emotional stance influence each other. Opening the hands can accompany a choice to meet the moment without requiring agreement, passivity, or surrendering a boundary.

references.title: DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015)

entries.short_definition: A relaxed, open-hand posture used to support willingness.

entries.definition: In DBT, willingness means participating in the situation and doing what is needed, guided by Wise Mind rather than rigid resistance. In ACT, it includes making room for discomfort in the service of values. Neither meaning requires obedience, approval of harm, or abandoning boundaries.

entries.short_definition: Readiness to engage with experience and choose a useful response despite discomfort.

entries.definition: Wise Mind is a DBT concept for the integrated perspective that draws on both emotional experience and reasonable thinking. It supports noticing what is true, what matters, and what an effective next step may be.

references.author: Marsha M. Linehan
references.title: DBT Skills Training Handouts and Worksheets, Second Edition (2015)

entries.short_definition: Wise Mind is the integrated perspective that draws on both emotion and reason.
